title: Web-CogReasoner: Knowledge-Induced Reasoning for Web Agents
one_liner: Web agents reason better when taught structured knowledge in three layers: what things are, how they work, and how to use them.
lead: Web agents—bots that click and type to complete tasks on websites—struggle because they lack the organized knowledge humans have. This paper argues web agents need three kinds of structured knowledge taught in stages: facts about what exists, concepts about how things work, and procedures for actually doing things. The paper builds a dataset from 14 real websites, trains an agent called Web-CogReasoner using step-by-step reasoning where each step explicitly cites a fact or concept, and shows it outperforms existing agents, especially on new unseen tasks because the abstract concepts transfer.

problem.h2: Web agents without structured knowledge fail on reasoning tasks
paras: A web agent is a software bot that sees a website, reads the page layout, and clicks or types to complete a task. Existing agents see raw pixels and try to reason on the fly, like a person dropped into a foreign city with no map or street signs. They can solve simple click-here tasks, but when a website has many pages, conditional logic, or requires understanding how pieces relate, they get stuck. They have no durable knowledge to anchor their decisions to.

A beginner might try to solve this by giving the agent a written description of every website page before it acts. But that scales poorly—websites are huge, pages look different each time they load, and a flat list of facts does not teach the agent how to think. The agent ends up making the same blind guess repeatedly.

callout.html: Teach the agent three layers of knowledge—facts, concepts, and procedures—in a deliberate order, then anchor each reasoning step to that knowledge.

panels.title: 1. Blind agent
panels.caption: Agent sees pixels. No knowledge of how websites work.

panels.title: 2. Memorize facts
panels.caption: First layer: learn what buttons, links, and fields exist.

panels.title: 3. Understand concepts
panels.caption: Second layer: learn how things relate and flow together.

panels.title: 4. Learn procedures
panels.caption: Third layer: practice actual task steps anchored to knowledge.

panels.title: 5. Reasoned agent
panels.caption: Agent now reasons step-by-step from structured knowledge.

steps.text: Gather facts, concepts, and procedures from 14 real websites.
Train agent to memorize facts and understand concepts in isolation.
Train agent to reason step-by-step using facts and concepts to guide action.
Each step outputs explicit reasoning tied to the knowledge layers.
Test on known tasks, new unseen tasks, and knowledge-intensive tasks separately.

object.h2: What the paper changes: knowledge layers in training order
paras: Instead of throwing all data at a web agent and hoping it learns, this paper teaches in stages: first isolated facts, then concepts, then procedures grounded in both. Each stage has its own training data and objective.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: knowledge structure maturity
hidden.name: knowledge layers present and used
paras: This paper measures what it calls the knowledge structure of a web agent—how many layers of knowledge it actually holds and can use. This is not one number but three: does the agent know facts (what is on the page), concepts (how things relate), and procedures (how to chain actions). The paper estimates this by checking if the agent can successfully reason through tasks that require each layer. A task needing only facts is easy; a task needing all three layers together is hard.

The paper operationalizes this through step-by-step reasoning outputs: if the agent explicitly writes out which fact or concept justifies each action, and if that reasoning is grounded in the training data, the knowledge is truly there. Without this anchoring, the agent is just pattern-matching.

heat.caption: Darker means the layer is more strongly used in reasoning for that task.

reads.html: If the agent can explain why it clicked, it has real knowledge.
The agent outputs knowledge-grounded Chain-of-Thought: each reasoning step explicitly cites a fact or concept from training.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: layered teaching creates durable anchors
paras: Human reasoning does not happen all at once. We first learn what exists (facts), then how things work (concepts), then how to solve real problems (procedures). Teaching a web agent the same way gives it stable anchors. When the agent later sees a new website or task, it can reason from these anchors instead of starting from scratch, because the anchors are abstract enough to apply to any website, not specific to one site.

Here is the causal chain: First, the agent memorizes facts—UI elements, labels, their positions. This creates a vocabulary it shares with the training data. Second, in Phase 1 training, the agent learns concepts by seeing repeated patterns: a search bar always leads to results after typing (input causes output), buttons always open menus when clicked (action causes visibility change), pages always flow forward (one page leads to another). These concepts are abstract patterns that repeat across different websites, so the agent picks them up from the data. Third, in Phase 2, it learns procedures: when given a goal, chain the concepts together step-by-step, and write out your reasoning tied to a concept each time. This step-by-step writing forces the agent to stay honest. If it invokes a concept that was never in the training data, the reasoning breaks. By requiring explicit reasoning anchored to the knowledge layers, the paper prevents the agent from hallucinating or guessing.

stages.s: Look up relevant facts from training
Chain concepts step-by-step, write reasoning each time

math.h2: How the three layers feed each reasoning step
math.equation: P(action_t | task, screen) = sum_k w_k * P(concept_k | state_t) where concept_k is grounded in factual_knowledge
symbols: the click or type at step t
a trained concept like trigger menu or find results
weight on how relevant that concept is

worked.title: A tiny worked example: finding an Apple Store
lines: User goal: Find Apple Stores near ZIP 90028.
Step 1 fact: A search bar is on the page. Concept: search bars find things. Weight: 0.8. Decision: Type the ZIP code.
Step 2 screen shows results. Fact: A stores link is labeled Find a Store. Concept: labeled links open pages. Weight: 0.9. Decision: Click Find a Store.
Step 3 screen shows a form. Fact: A text field is labeled ZIP code. Concept: text fields accept input. Weight: 0.8. Decision: Type 90028.
Each step ties a fact on the screen to a learned concept to produce an action. Without that reasoning, the agent is blind.

math.note: The equation shows that each action is a weighted sum of concepts, and each concept is grounded in facts the agent learned during Phase 1.

bars.h2: Performance: structured knowledge on different task types

charts.title: Tasks needing facts only
charts.note: Both agents can find elements. New agent is slightly better because it has cleaner fact representations.

charts.title: Tasks needing concepts and procedures
charts.note: Gap widens: existing agents lack structured concepts. Web-CogReasoner's layered training is decisive.

charts.title: New unseen websites
charts.note: On truly new tasks, the advantage is greatest. Abstract concepts trained on known sites transfer; raw pattern-matching does not.

items.html: If the agent memorizes facts that do not transfer—like exact pixel positions instead of semantic labels—Phase 2 and 3 will fail. The whole stack collapses.

If Phase 2 learns narrow patterns tied to specific websites, concepts do not transfer to new sites. The agent needs abstract concepts like trigger navigation or find results, not website-specific patterns.

items.b: Reasoning step is not truly grounded.
items.html: If the agent writes reasoning that sounds good but does not actually cite a fact or concept from training, it is hallucinating. The paper prevents this by requiring explicit citations.
Facts are semantic (button labeled X), concepts are abstract (buttons open menus), procedures chain them step-by-step with explicit reasoning. Transfer to new sites becomes reliable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build an agent trained on one set of 14 websites. Then show it a website from that set, and a completely new website never seen during training. Run the same task on both. Compare the step-by-step reasoning outputs. On the trained website, count how many reasoning steps cite facts and concepts from the training data. On the unseen website, do the same. The paper's claim is that the unseen website will still use the learned concepts correctly, because they are abstract enough to transfer.
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: abstract structured knowledge transfers to new sites; raw pattern-matching does not.
